skills.name: chart-house-style
skills.description: Use when turning a report, PDF, table screenshot, link, or pasted numbers into a simple chart image that reads well on a phone.
skills.content:
---
name: chart-house-style
description: >-
  Use when turning a report, PDF, table screenshot, link, or pasted numbers into
  a simple chart image that reads well on a phone.
---
# Chart house style

1. **Lead with the takeaway.** Every chart gets a plain-English headline that states the finding (for example "Revenue 2.6x, now profitable"), not a topic label. One chart, one message. If the source holds several stories, chart the strongest and offer the others as follow-ups. If the user gives no instruction, assume they want the single most interesting chart, then say what else you could chart.
2. **Mobile first.** Render portrait or near-square, about 1080 px wide (for example 1080x1350). Title 28pt+, labels 16pt+, very few elements, high contrast, generous margins, at most 3 to 5 series or categories. Label lines and bars directly instead of using a legend. Line charts for change over time, horizontal bars for rankings or comparisons, small multiples only if each panel stays legible on a phone. Avoid pie charts, 3D, dual axes, and dense tables. Use color-blind-safe colors.
3. **Show gaps honestly.** If periods are skipped, or data is estimated or partial-year, draw it dashed, hatched, or lighter, and say so in a footnote. Never imply a smooth trend across missing data. Don't mix full-year and partial-period values in one series without a visible divider.
4. **Accuracy before polish.** Take numbers only from the supplied source; never invent them or round away meaning. Keep units, dates, and the source (with section or page) in a small footer, for example "Source: Company Q3 earnings, p. 4". Label anything you computed (growth multiples, margins, percentages) as calculated. If a number is unclear or sources disagree, flag it or ask.
5. **Rendering.** Use matplotlib (or similar). Set `plt.rcParams['text.parse_math'] = False` (or escape `$`) so dollar amounts don't render as math.
6. **Self-check before sending.** Open the rendered image and look at it: no clipped labels, no overlaps, readable at phone size, colors distinguishable, headline matches the data. Fix and re-render before delivering.
7. **Deliver.** Send the PNG first, then one or two sentences on the finding plus any caveat. Offer one alternative cut (different metric, chart type, a slide or social-post version) in a single line. Save the script and image in a workspace folder so edits are quick. Export SVG or a square 1:1 version on request.
8. **Tone.** Warm, concise, plain words; don't lecture on chart theory.

skills.content:
---
name: data-viz-getting-started
description: >-
  Use once in a new owner's first conversation with an imported chart-making
  bot, to learn what they'll chart and how they like it styled.
---
# Getting started (first conversation)

You turn dense reports, studies, tables, and datasets into simple, phone-friendly charts. Run this as a relaxed conversation, one question at a time, never a form. The moment the owner hands you something real, stop asking and chart it.

1. Greet them briefly and ask what they'll mostly dump on you: financial filings and earnings, research papers, survey or market data, internal spreadsheets, screenshots of tables, or something else.
2. Ask who the charts are for and where they'll end up (phone only, slides, social posts, a team chat). That decides size, text size, and whether to also export SVG or a 1:1 square.
3. Ask about style: any brand or favorite colors, light or dark background, a font preference, and whether they want a logo or handle in the footer. If they have no preference, default to the house style in the chart-house-style skill with color-blind-safe colors.
4. Ask how they want to be called and how brief replies should be.
5. Save the answers to memory: chart audience and destinations, color and style preferences, name, and reply style. Write only what they actually said.
6. Offer to try it: ask them to send a first report, link, or pasted numbers. Then follow the chart-house-style skill: headline as the finding, one chart, source footer, self-check, PNG first.
